description: Day Five DotPy fictional admin training
narration: Welcome back to DotPy, and welcome to Day Five of Excel Intermediate to Master. Today we finish the programme by making administrative reporting repeatable and reliable. On Day Four we built management summaries and dashboards. On Day Five we prepare messy imports, combine them, verify employee details, test a refresh, automate safe presentation steps, and critically review an AI formula. We will use your Day Five Practical workbook, with fictional South African administrative data and rand amounts. Keep it open beside this video. This is a full guided teaching lesson: pause for the exercises, complete them yourself, and resume when you are ready.

Here is our route for the day. Exercise G1 deals with Power Query imports and data types. G2 covers appending two files, removing duplicate trip identifiers, and merging employee names. G3 proves that adding three new trips changes a refreshed result by exactly the right amount. G4 explores a recorded formatting macro and a small automation script. G5 checks a deliberately flawed AI-generated overdue formula and prepares a professional handover. We will finish with an integrated practical challenge. You do not need to memorise button names. You need to know the purpose of each transformation and how to test the result.

Open D5 Practical, not the Day Four workbook. Your source data sits in the Import A, Import B, Employees and Refresh Rows tabs. There is also a Monthly report, a Dashboard, Settings and Notes. The exercise uses a fixed reporting date of the thirtieth of September twenty twenty-six, and every amount is fictional. Before making changes, save a learner copy and preserve the untouched original. The source sheets are deliberately imperfect: some department names contain unnecessary spaces, money is stored as text beginning with the letter R, and the two imported batches contain repeated trips.

A very important distinction before we start. The original Day Five assessment uses Microsoft Excel desktop Power Query and VBA macros. Google Sheets does not contain Excel Power Query, its M language query editor, or the VBA editor. Since our recent lessons have used Google Sheets, I will teach the same data-cleaning reasoning and show Sheets-native formula and Apps Script alternatives. I will label the Excel-only steps clearly rather than inventing Google Sheets menus. If your assessment must show an actual installed qTravel Power Query, complete that part in the Microsoft Excel desktop application, or follow your facilitator’s approved alternative.

Imagine an executive office receives two travel exports from different departments. One contains extra spaces and another includes amounts as text, for example R space one thousand four hundred and eighty point zero zero. If you paste the rows directly into a management report, SUM may ignore text and a pivot may split Finance from Finance with a trailing space. The correct approach is a repeatable cleaning pipeline. Preserve the original data, standardise field names and types, and produce a separate clean result. Never correct a query output manually and assume that the correction will survive a refresh. Record how you transformed every field.

In your actual workbook, Import A has forty-five trip records and Import B has forty-seven. Both use the same six columns: Trip ID, Date, Employee ID, Department, Approval, and Amount Text. They represent two batches of fictional administrative travel transactions. The total before deduplication is ninety-two rows. But two of those rows are deliberately exact repeats, so the finished report must contain ninety unique trips. Take a moment to find the column headers on both tabs and compare their order. Before combining datasets, you must understand whether matching column names really mean matching concepts.

Look at Trip TR zero zero one in the first data row of Import A. It has the date twenty twenty-six dash zero four dash zero one, employee identifier E zero zero one, and department shown with spaces around Executive. Approval is Pending. Its Amount Text entry is R space fourteen eighty point zero zero. This is not yet a reliable numeric amount. We want a clean department called Executive, a genuine date value, and an amount of one thousand four hundred and eighty rand that SUM can calculate. The row identifier must stay exactly the same throughout this process.

If you are using Windows desktop Excel for the original assessed exercise, click inside the Import A table. Use Data, then From Table or Range under Get and Transform. The Power Query editor opens with the selected table. In the Queries pane, rename the query qA. Inspect each field’s data type icon. The Applied Steps panel shows the sequence of changes that Power Query will repeat later. Do not confuse changing a display format in Excel with changing a field’s actual type inside Power Query. They are different operations. We will repeat this later for Import B and name that second query qB.

Department values contain extra spaces. In Excel Power Query, select Department and use Transform, Format, Trim. The value space Finance space becomes Finance. That matters because a pivot table sees different character strings as different categories. In Google Sheets, a parallel exercise is the TRIM function: equals TRIM open bracket D two close bracket. Press Enter and confirm that Executive has no leading or trailing spaces. Fill down in a separate clean column. On the full column you can also use ARRAYFORMULA with TRIM, but first understand the single-row transformation. Notice that the original value remains unchanged in the source.

The source amount includes a currency prefix, so we must convert it to an actual number, not merely change its appearance. In Power Query, replace the R prefix with nothing, trim, and change the type to Decimal Number. In Google Sheets, try equals VALUE open bracket REGEXREPLACE open bracket F two comma quotation marks caret open square bracket zero through nine point close square bracket comma quotation marks, quotation marks quotation marks close bracket close bracket. For the provided positive example, this strips nonnumeric characters and returns fourteen eighty. Format the result as South African rand separately. For genuine accounting data, handle negative signs and locale explicitly.

The raw Date column contains ISO-formatted text, like twenty twenty-six dash zero four dash zero one. We need a genuine spreadsheet date, because monthly grouping and comparison depend on the stored value, not the way it looks. In Power Query choose Date data type, with the appropriate locale if prompted. In Google Sheets a stable manual example extracts year, month and day and passes them into DATE. After conversion, change the display to a human-readable date format and sort a few rows. A real date will sort and compare correctly; a text date can produce subtle reporting errors. Do not silently guess day-month order.

A repeatable transformation should be transparent. First read the source, second trim the Department values, third convert Amount Text to a numeric Amount, and fourth interpret Date as an actual date. In Excel the Applied Steps pane should show those operations; in Google Sheets keep calculated clean columns or a separate staging sheet, clearly labelled. If a value fails, identify the exact step rather than patching the final report. Give the new amount field the unambiguous name Amount, so readers know it is money, not the original string. Keep the raw AmountText as evidence where required.

Let's pause over a dangerous misunderstanding. If I select a text value and format the cell as Currency, Google Sheets or Excel may not change the value into a number. The visual presentation can look like money while SUM still ignores it. A trustworthy test uses ISNUMBER on the cleaned Amount cell. If that returns TRUE, the value can participate in arithmetic. Also add two sample rows by hand and compare their sum with the spreadsheet result. In Power Query, check that the column-type indicator explicitly shows Decimal Number rather than Text. The underlying value is what matters, not the appearance on screen.

The training data is intentionally tidy enough to clean using a simple expression, but real imports may contain hidden problems. Some amounts might have a comma decimal separator, an unexpected currency symbol, a minus sign, or an empty value. If you erase every character except digits and points without checking those cases, you can silently change the meaning. That is why our Google Sheets REGEXREPLACE formula is labelled as a positive-number exercise example, not a universal accounting parser. A robust production transformation must define locale, negative values and blanks; then reject exceptions for review. Document that limitation in your handover rather than assuming every future month will look identical.

Now check your first result before proceeding. Import A must have forty-five data rows and Import B forty-seven. We do not deduct duplicates inside each individual batch at this stage. The number ninety-two refers to the combined rows before removing the two exact repeats. Confirm the clean Amount field really is numeric by summing a few examples. Compare one original text value with its clean amount. If the row count changed during cleaning, investigate blanks, headers, or accidental filtering. A good data pipeline does not just look tidy; it can explain which rows came in and why none went missing.

Now exercise G2 combines the datasets. Append means stacking rows from the same type of table. If April records arrive in one file and May records arrive in another, appending puts them underneath one another. Merge means joining columns from another table using a matching key, such as Employee ID. We need both operations for Day Five. First append Import A and Import B. Then remove exact duplicate trip identifiers. Only after we have a stable travel table do we bring in employee names. If you reverse the logic or use the wrong key, you can accidentally multiply or lose rows.

In the Power Query editor, after creating qA and qB as connection-only queries, choose Home, Append Queries as New. Select the two input queries and name the new query qTravel. The combined view should show ninety-two rows before deduplication. Make sure the same fields have compatible types in both sources, especially Date and Amount. Append matches columns by name, so a misspelt header can create a separate column full of blanks. Don't simply look at the first five rows: check row count, column count, and values from both the start and end of the combined result.

Google Sheets does not have Excel's Power Query Append Queries button. A Sheets-native alternative is VSTACK, which places the second range below the first. Use FILTER to exclude blank trailing rows before stacking. Conceptually, the first FILTER selects all occupied data rows from Import A, and the second selects all occupied data rows from Import B. VSTACK then gives a ninety-two-row combined output. When you work with the raw columns, remember that Department, Date and AmountText still need cleaning in a separate stage. A dynamic source range is important if you want later refresh rows to flow in automatically.

Here is the exact trap in your workbook. Trip TR zero zero three and trip TR zero zero six each appear twice across the imported batches. They are exact repeated records, not separate journeys. Both copies have the same trip identifier and accompanying details. If we simply sum all ninety-two rows, those two trips are counted twice and the report exaggerates expenditure. Look for the duplicated Trip IDs and compare every other field before deleting one. In an operational dataset, repeated IDs can have conflicting dates or amounts. Those need an exception report, not an automatic arbitrary choice.

In Power Query, select the TripID field and choose Remove Duplicates. The result should contain ninety unique trips. Here it is safe because the repeated details agree. In Google Sheets you can use UNIQUE on the combined table to drop completely identical rows. Be careful: UNIQUE across six columns only removes rows that match in all six fields. If two rows share a TripID but different amounts, they will both remain. For a real business process, flag that conflict and ask for a documented resolution rule. Every cleaning step must be explainable to someone who did not build the original workbook.

Here is the conceptual Google Sheets formula for our exact-match training records. Wrap the combined two-filter VSTACK result in UNIQUE. The output spills from the top-left formula cell, so keep the destination range empty. If the output says an array could not expand, clear the blocking cells rather than replacing the formula with pasted values. Count the resulting Trip IDs with COUNTA and confirm ninety. You are not deleting anything from Import A or Import B; the formula produces a new view. That makes it easy to prove your source data is preserved. Remember that a UNIQUE operation cannot resolve conflicting records.

Next, we want a readable employee name alongside each trip. The travel imports have EmployeeID, such as E zero zero one. The Employees sheet maps that identifier to a person’s training name. Do not join on a person’s given name because names can repeat or change. Employee ID is the stable key in this exercise. One sample match is E zero zero one to Lindiwe Dube. Another is E zero zero two to Sipho Mokoena. The workbook has fifteen employee reference records. Before merging, check that each identifier appears only once on the employee list. Otherwise a join might create extra travel rows.

Back in the Excel Power Query interface, create qEmployees from the Employees table. Select qTravel, choose Merge Queries, select qEmployees, and match the EmployeeID column in both tables. Choose Left Outer, meaning keep all records from the travel table even if no employee matches. Expand the name column and label it EmployeeName. Why not an Inner join? Because an inner join can quietly drop a trip with an unknown employee identifier. We want exceptions to remain visible, not to disappear. After the merge, the number of unique travel rows should still be ninety, and every training Employee ID should have a matching name.

For Google Sheets, use a lookup formula rather than Excel's Merge Queries dialog. If Employee ID is in C two, use INDEX on Employees column B and MATCH on Employees column A with exact match. Wrap it in IFNA so an unknown identifier becomes an explicit word like UNMATCHED instead of a hidden error. For E zero zero one the expected result is Lindiwe Dube. Copy the lookup down the clean table. Count any UNMATCHED values. They should be zero for our original training data. Do not turn an unmatched employee into an empty label, because the missing match is precisely the control information you need.

Here is a useful boundary test. On a disposable copy, change one travel EmployeeID to E nine nine nine, which does not appear on the employee reference sheet. A left outer merge keeps the travel row but leaves its employee name unmatched. A lookup with IFNA shows UNMATCHED. An inner join might discard the trip completely, causing your row count and expenditure total to fall without a conspicuous error. That is why our quality checklist checks both unique trip count and unmatched join count. Restore the genuine identifier afterward. Never leave a deliberately corrupted test row inside the source workbook you intend to submit.

Let's trace one record from beginning to end. Trip TR zero zero one starts in Import A with Employee ID E zero zero one, amount text R space fourteen eighty, and Department padded by spaces. After cleaning, its Department becomes Executive, the Amount is the number fourteen eighty, and its Date is a valid date. The employee reference then adds Lindiwe Dube. Because this trip has a unique identifier it remains in the deduplicated result. Its Approval remains Pending. Nothing in this data pipeline should change an approval decision: we are standardising the record for reporting, not authorising expenditure. Try tracing one other trip in your workbook.

A single grand total can match while department allocation is wrong. For a stronger check, summarise the clean travel output by department and compare the all-status department totals from Day Four: Executive is one hundred and seven thousand four hundred rand. Finance is one hundred and seven thousand one hundred and eighty rand. Operations is one hundred and six thousand nine hundred and sixty rand. Those three figures add to three hundred and twenty-one thousand five hundred and forty rand. If the overall total is correct but Finance is too high and Executive too low, investigate department cleaning or join logic. We should verify category assignments, not only the final sum.

Now we reach the control that matters most. After cleaning, stacking, removing the exact duplicates and adding employee names, the qTravel result must show ninety unique trips. The Amount total must be three hundred and twenty-one thousand five hundred and forty rand, equal to the all-status travel amount from the earlier lessons. There should be no unmatched employee identifiers. These three checks answer different questions. Ninety checks completeness, the rand total checks values, and zero unmatched checks reference integrity. A report can pass one check and fail another, so do not accept a green-looking dashboard without doing all three.

Exercise G3 asks a simple question: can the workbook update itself correctly when the source receives new records? A refresh button is not proof on its own. You must know the starting position, add a known test change, run the refresh or recomputation, and measure what changed. Our Day Five Practical workbook includes three additional test trips on RefreshRows. They are deliberately small enough to verify by hand. Keep a pre-test copy of the original workbook and write down the original row count and amount. The refresh test is not complete until you can explain why the new totals are different.

Start with the current clean result, not a guessed number. We confirmed ninety unique trips and three hundred and twenty-one thousand five hundred and forty rand. In your Notes sheet record those two numbers with a label saying before refresh. Also record the reporting date, the source tables, and whether any filter is active. If you compare an approved-only result with an all-status result, the difference is not necessarily a refresh failure; it may be a filter mismatch. Our Day Five control uses all recorded travel, including Approved and Pending. Do not change that population halfway through the test.

Look at the RefreshRows tab. It contains exactly three fictional new records. TR dash NEW dash one belongs to Executive and has an approved amount of one thousand five hundred rand. TR dash NEW dash two belongs to Finance and is two thousand five hundred. TR dash NEW dash three belongs to Operations and is three thousand five hundred. All three use valid employee identifiers and late-September dates. Add their amounts manually: fifteen hundred plus twenty-five hundred plus thirty-five hundred equals seven thousand five hundred rand. That manual calculation is our independent expected change, before we press any refresh button.

In desktop Excel, the Power Query qTravel source points to the named Import tables. Copy the three RefreshRows records into the next rows inside the tblImportB table, not merely below an unrelated range. When Excel tables expand, Power Query can read the new records during Refresh All. Before refreshing, check Table Design and verify the table range includes those three rows. If the new data sit outside the named table, pressing Refresh All may do absolutely nothing. That is a source-range problem, not necessarily a query problem. Keep the worksheet’s field order and types identical to the original data.

In Google Sheets, a properly designed VSTACK and FILTER formula can include new rows automatically if its source ranges extend through the added records. If you hard-code Import B from row two to row forty-eight, pasting new records at rows forty-nine through fifty-one will leave them out. That would make the result appear unchanged. For this lesson, keep dynamic source ranges like A two through F, filtered where column A is not blank. Then check whether the clean columns also extend. If they do not, adjust the calculations consistently. Always validate the number of rows and the sum after the update.

Let's use the three new records to make a stronger prediction before refreshing. Executive gains one thousand five hundred rand. Finance gains two thousand five hundred. Operations gains three thousand five hundred. That means the department totals after refresh should become Executive one hundred and eight thousand nine hundred, Finance one hundred and nine thousand six hundred and eighty, and Operations one hundred and ten thousand four hundred and sixty. Add those numbers: they give three hundred and twenty-nine thousand and forty rand. Department control totals help us catch a misclassified row, even when the overall sum is correct. You can record this optional check in Notes.

All three refresh rows are dated in September twenty twenty-six. If your monthly summary uses trip date and filters to Approved, the September approved travel amount should rise by seven thousand five hundred rand, because all three new records are Approved. Other months should remain unchanged. This test matters because a pipeline can import the right number of records but assign them to the wrong month if it misreads text dates. Use an actual date value and a month boundary based on the first day of September and the first day of October. If the month changes unexpectedly, inspect the date conversion and locale settings.

Our predicted result is now straightforward. Ninety previous unique trips plus three new ones equals ninety-three. Three hundred and twenty-one thousand five hundred and forty rand plus seven thousand five hundred gives three hundred and twenty-nine thousand and forty rand. These values are the Day Five answer checks after the three test records enter the source. If you see ninety-three but the sum is wrong, inspect amount conversion, blank values, and duplicate handling. If you see ninety, check whether the source grew. If you see ninety-five, inspect the two deliberate duplicate trips again. Diagnose the failed control rather than changing the expected number.

Here is the second essential test. Without adding any more rows, run Refresh All in Excel again or allow the Google Sheets formulas to recalculate. The result must stay at ninety-three trips and three hundred and twenty-nine thousand and forty rand. It must not grow by another three rows or another seven thousand five hundred rand. That behavior is called idempotence: running the same operation on unchanged input does not change the result. It is especially important for monthly reporting, where a well-meaning staff member may refresh repeatedly. If every run appends copies to the output, that is a dangerous design error.

Let's learn the four most common reasons a repeatable import breaks. First, the source path may point to a colleague’s desktop or a file that moved. Second, table names or column headings may change between months. Third, a new field value may have the wrong data type, such as a malformed date or a text amount. Fourth, the new rows may sit outside the named source range. In every case, work backward through the pipeline. Do not turn off checks just to make the report load. Create an exception list, fix the source or the documented transformation, and rerun the count and sum validations.

Imagine a new private secretary takes over this report next month. Could that person update it without calling you? A good four-step checklist says where the approved source tables live, which query or formula to refresh, what totals must be checked, and where to record exceptions. Our example might read: receive and validate monthly exports; run the import transformation; compare unique Trip IDs and total Amount with independent controls; then publish only after unmatched employees and duplicate conflicts have been reviewed. Store the last refresh date and the name of the reviewer in Notes. These controls are part of the work, not optional decoration.

Exercise G4 looks at automation, but our first rule is important: automate stable, repeatable actions, not uncertain business judgments. Formatting a monthly header the same way every time is a sensible beginner task. Deleting questionable employee records or approving travel is not. Excel desktop offers recorded macros and VBA procedures. Google Sheets offers macros and Apps Script based on JavaScript. These technologies differ, but the control principles are the same. Define one safe operation, record what it changes, test it on a copy, and confirm it does not silently alter data values or create duplicate records. Never let automation hide an exception.

For learners completing the Windows Excel assessment, first save a separate macro-enabled copy with the xlsm extension. Open the Developer tab if your organisation permits it. Select Record Macro, name your formatting routine FormatPractice, then on the Monthly sheet select the report header cells A one through H one. Make the header bold, apply a dark fill and white text, then stop recording. Manually undo those style changes and run the recorded macro to check the result. The goal is to reproduce formatting without changing the report’s counts or currency values. Do not weaken organisational macro security settings to finish an exercise.

The exercise pack contains an optional VBA module named AdminAutomation. A procedure such as FormatMonthly should refer to the intended workbook and sheet rather than relying on whatever window is active. In VBA, ThisWorkbook means the workbook containing the code; ActiveWorkbook means whichever workbook happens to have focus. The distinction prevents formatting the wrong file. Before importing any macro, read its statements, check the sheet names, and save a clean backup. Our practice macro should change style only. A macro-enabled file extension is not a safety guarantee, and Excel for the web cannot run VBA procedures like the Windows desktop application does.

For the Google Sheets route, we can achieve the same harmless formatting task using Apps Script. Open Extensions, Apps Script, in a training copy if your school or employer allows scripts. The code obtains the active spreadsheet, looks up the Monthly sheet by name, selects A one through H one, and applies bold text, a dark navy background and white lettering. This is not VBA; it is JavaScript running in the Google Workspace environment. Before granting permissions, review exactly what the script accesses. Run it only in a workbook you control. If your organisation blocks scripts, document the manual formatting sequence instead.

Here is the complete beginner-level idea in Apps Script. A function named formatMonthly obtains a worksheet called Monthly, selects the header range, and then sets a background color, white font and bold weight. Notice that no line inserts or deletes records, changes a number, or modifies an approval status. A formatter should be idempotent: running it twice leaves the same presentation and source values. If your sheet is named differently, the lookup returns no sheet and you must fix the name. Never paste scripts from an AI tool into a sensitive organisation workbook without review and permission.

Imagine you click a completely different cell before running a formatting macro. If the automation always formats whatever range happens to be selected, the wrong part of the workbook might change. That is why our safe Apps Script uses getSheetByName and getRange, and why the optional VBA procedure uses ThisWorkbook and a named worksheet. Explicit targets are easier to test than assumptions about which tab is active. Keep your automation as small as possible. A formatter for Monthly A one through H one should never refer to the Travel source, the Actions register or employee identifiers. One precise action is better than a magical but dangerous script.

After running the macro or Apps Script, inspect the report. Does it look right? More importantly, are the underlying numbers unchanged? Check a few cells in the Monthly report against their pre-run values, then run the formatter a second time. The formatting should remain the same. No extra rows should appear, and no formula should have been replaced with a hard-coded number. Document the test in Notes: script name, target range, expected visual change, values before and after, and the result. If you cannot execute a script because of organisational policy, use a manual formatting checklist and explain why that alternative is appropriate.

Our final skills block is AI-assisted productivity. A good assistant can explain a formula, suggest a structured report, or help identify an edge case. It does not automatically know the rules of your organisation. Even a confident-sounding formula can flag completed actions as overdue, omit a boundary date, or use the wrong column. We will inspect one deliberately flawed overdue suggestion from the assessment pack. You can complete this exercise without a paid AI account: the incorrect formula is already supplied. Think like a reviewer. What is the precise business rule, and what examples would prove that the formula implements it correctly?

Here is the flawed suggestion. It compares the Due date in F two against the reporting date in Settings B two, and if it is older, returns Overdue. Otherwise it returns On track. That sounds plausible, but one critical condition is missing. The action may already be marked Complete in H two. A completed action with an old due date should not be flagged as currently overdue. The formula also needs to treat due today differently from due yesterday, and blank due dates need a documented rule. Before editing the expression, write the correct sentence in plain English: flag only non-complete actions whose due date is earlier than the report date.

The corrected logic uses AND. The action is overdue only if Status is not Complete, the due date is not blank, and the due date is strictly earlier than the reporting date. In Google Sheets and modern Excel, we can write equals IF of AND H two not equal Complete, F two not equal empty, F two less than Settings B two, then Overdue, otherwise On track. Notice the strict less-than sign: due today is not overdue. Notice also that the report date is an absolute reference, with dollar signs before B and two, so it does not move when copied down. This is a business-rule correction, not simply a syntax correction.

Let us test the corrected formula on the fixed report date, thirtieth September twenty twenty-six. Case one: a Complete action with a due date in the past. It should say On track for our simple open-overdue flag, not Overdue. Case two: an Open action due exactly on the report date. It should say On track, because the date is not earlier. Case three: an Open action due yesterday. It should say Overdue. Write expected results before calculating. You can add an optional fourth case with a blank date and confirm that your blank-date rule prevents a misleading flag. These small tests catch errors faster than scanning a huge register.

When using an approved AI tool, specify the exact cells and rules rather than asking for a generic overdue formula. A strong prompt says: In Google Sheets, Due is column F, Status is column H, and the report date is Settings B two. Return Overdue only when Status is not Complete, Due is present, and Due is earlier than the reporting date. Otherwise return On track. Keep the report-date reference fixed when copying down, and supply three boundary tests. The prompt makes assumptions explicit, but you must still test the returned formula against your workbook. Never mistake a detailed AI explanation for proof that the calculation is correct.

We are working with fictional records for good reason. Government administration can involve sensitive correspondence, staffing details, private contact information and executive decisions. Never paste real case files, identification numbers, private emails, beneficiary details or confidential meeting notes into an unapproved AI service. If you need formula help, use a made-up example with the same column structure and safe sample values. Ask your organisation which AI tools and data-handling rules are approved. You can also do the entire exercise offline by reviewing the flawed formula provided in the workbook materials. Responsible use means protecting data as well as getting the right answer.

Let's connect each boundary case to the corrected formula. When Status equals Complete, the condition H two not equal Complete is FALSE, so AND is false even if the due date was last week. When an Open action is due today, the comparison F two less than the report date is FALSE because the dates are equal. When an Open action was due yesterday, the status test, nonblank test and date comparison all return TRUE. Only then does the formula return Overdue. Testing each condition separately is an effective way to understand a compound formula and to spot a missing business rule.

A report is not finished when it looks attractive on your computer. Another colleague should be able to reproduce it after you leave. Write a five-line handover: where the incoming source files or tables are stored; the order of cleaning, appending, deduplicating and merging; the reporting date and how it is updated; the definitions of the dashboard measures; and how exceptions are recorded or escalated. Add the last verified row count and amount total. Make clear whether the workbook depends on desktop Excel Power Query and VBA or on Google Sheets formulas and Apps Script. That small detail can save the next administrator hours of confusion.

Now bring everything together. Using a fresh learner copy, clean the two imported batches, combine them into one result, remove the two repeated trips, and match employee names. Verify ninety unique trips and a total of three hundred and twenty-one thousand five hundred and forty rand before refresh. Then append the three RefreshRows and prove a count of ninety-three and a total of three hundred and twenty-nine thousand and forty rand. Repeat the refresh without new input and prove the total does not change. Format your Monthly header with an approved macro or manual procedure. Finally correct the overdue formula and document your handover and evidence in Notes.

Before looking at the answers, ask yourself these five questions. Why must AmountText become a numeric Amount? What is the difference between append and merge? Why should the merge keep all travel rows, even when an employee is missing? What proves the refresh is repeatable? And why does the first AI overdue formula fail for a completed action? Say your explanations out loud, not just the formulas. The goal of this course is not to memorise a click path. It is to know which data you are using, how the result was produced, and what would make that result unsafe to report to management.

The final verification board should be familiar now. Import A has forty-five records, Import B has forty-seven, and their raw append contains ninety-two. Removing two exact duplicates gives ninety unique Trip IDs. The combined Amount sum is three hundred and twenty-one thousand five hundred and forty rand. Adding the three approved refresh records increases the count to ninety-three and the sum by seven thousand five hundred, to three hundred and twenty-nine thousand and forty rand. The employee lookup should have zero unmatched identifiers for the original training data. A second refresh must leave the answer unchanged. Screenshot or record each check in your learner evidence.

Save the final Day Five learner workbook with your assigned learner number. Follow your facilitator’s assessment instructions for the optional macro-enabled xlsm copy. Your Notes should identify at least one before-and-after source transformation, the two repeated trip identifiers, the baseline and post-refresh totals, and the AI formula’s three boundary tests. Include a brief handover for the next administrator. Do not submit temporary E nine nine nine test records or an unapproved automation script. For learners working in Google Sheets, include equivalent formula evidence and explain that native Power Query or VBA tasks require desktop Excel. The objective is a defensible, shareable process.

Congratulations. You have completed the final Day Five teaching lesson. Over the week you progressed from reliable administrative records to accurate formulas, budget analysis, PivotTables, dashboards, repeatable data preparation, automation and responsible AI review. The strongest spreadsheet professional is not the person who knows the largest number of functions. It is the person who can explain where a number came from, reproduce it, test it against an independent control, and hand over the process safely. Keep practising with your fictional Day Five workbook, and ask questions whenever a result surprises you. This has been DotPy, the dot that matters. Thank you for learning with us.
